entries.title: The Funniest Books of 2026, recommended by Sophie Ratcliffe
entries.summary: Every year, the judges of the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for Comic Fiction select the funniest novel published in the past twelve months. In 2026, finalists include a Booker-nominated book about a man in a black bag and a Regency rom-com with a very modern sensibility. Judge, academic and author Sophie Ratcliffe talks us through the six-book shortlist. This interview appeared first on Five
entries.content:
Thank you for talking to us about the six-book shortlist for the 2026 Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for comic fiction. I wonder: is judging humorous writing unusually difficult?

Yes, I think there is a difficulty. I guess what different people find funny or ‘comic’ is pretty subjective. It sounds a touch grave to say that it feels like a responsibility, but it is. We were all trying to come to these books with as open a mind as possible about the varieties of humour that we might encounter. We, as a panel, were looking for books that would make us laugh out loud, but were were also open to those that made us smile or raise an eyebrow, which plunged us into the absurd and grotesque, or the dry and the wry…

Also, crucially, we wanted books that were exceptionally well-written. My own acid test for any really great book – particularly a great comic or joy-giving book – is that I want to press it into the hands of someone who, say, tells me they are going into hospital and need something good to read. Maybe that sounds vague, but these were the rough ingredients of the recipe we were looking for.

A funny book is not the same thing as a light read. They can be both, but a great funny book should still be a quality book.

That’s right. And when I look at the shortlist from this year, that comes through.

Let’s look at those books, one at a time. Can we start with A Good Person by Kirsten King? It features a modern-day hex.

I love this one. Here’s the plot. The heroine of this book breaks up with her boyfriend, who she spent quite a lot of time getting. She also works for a marketing company, and through her work encounters the ‘Wellness Witch’, a social influencer, who gives her the tools to put a ‘hex’ on her ex.

It’s very filmic – King is a screenwriter, and you can tell. I think what stands out in this one is the voice. It’s so good, full of very funny one-liners, which are integrated beautifully. It’s also a page-turner.

The title is A Good Person, and it is very thoughtful about ethics, carried with a light touch. It makes one think about what that means, to be a good person, and what it might be like to want to hex someone, and what to do with shame when things get out of control.

Then all of that is played through a sort of millennial angst about paying rent and having roommates. It’s a gorgeous piece of work: quite dark, very funny.

It’s a classic combination. Comedians are famously troubled. Is there a thread of darkness running through all of the books?

In many of them, yes. There’s quite a lot of trauma and darkness to negotiate in this list. But what the books have in common is that while the dark recesses of the soul might be pondered or traversed, the joke always lands at home. The thread these books have in common is that the comedy is entwined with kindness. They certainly don’t punch down.

Luke Kennard’s Black Bag also featured on the Booker Prize shortlist, which I was delighted to see. I think it’s great. Why did the Wodehouse Prize judges admire it?

Well, it made us all laugh out loud. That’s the first thing. I don’t know if that is the most important thing to say about it, but for this prize it is very important. It’s not a book that is safe to read on a train because you will spill your coffee. And, actually, there’s a fantastic scene involving a coffee mishap—

Yes!

It’s a really, really funny book. So the scenario is based on a real-life psychological experiment where a professor hired someone to wear a large, leather, full-body black bag around the campus of a university to see what happened. So that is clearly completely absurd. The person in this book who is performing as the black bag is a failed actor, and this ‘part’ becomes his starring role. We admired the huge comedy of the novel, but in its construction, Black Bag has really thought through this comic scenario and what it can tell us about what it means to make art, and what it is like to be a human being.

Again, this is a book that does not laugh at anyone, but rather at the predicament of what it means to be human. We also loved the physical comedy. The tiny details. The actor wearing the black bag immacs his lower legs to make sure that no one can work out whether he’s male or female. And he talks brilliantly to the visceral feeling of wearing hot, black leather. There are also interesting themes which emerge around another character who makes a living through livestreams and cryptocurrency. So this book makes us ponder the relationship between the virtual and the material.

It’s a very clever book, but with great humour. You’re physically wincing as you read. It’s masterly.

Well, we have a very different book up next. This is How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin. It’s a Regency rom-com. Tell us more.

One thing I want to highlight about this book is that it is gorgeously reflexive. It begins with the heroine reading a novel. The title too, is a riff on How to Lose a Guy in Ten Days, the Kate Hudson and Matthew McConaughey film.

Plotwise, it’s a Regency comedy in which both members of the couple are trying to break off an engagement, but modernity keeps poking its nose through the pages. You get a sense, almost, that they are wearing sneakerinas under their muslin frocks. It’s an enjoyable historical novel, but also a comedy about what it means to write historical fiction. It’s clever and quite delicious – probably the lightest book on the list.

I did want to give a shout out to some of the period descriptions: There’s a moment when Lydia takes a seat between a beef tremblant and a pigeon à la crapaudine. And there are descriptions of characters galloping ventre à terre, a Georgette Heyer term – if somebody really loves you, they will ride so that their horse’s belly is grazing the ground.

So, yes, romantic, but it’s a story not just about the characters but how we reimagine history. It laughs at, and with us, for wanting to revisit the past.

I love that. And the fondness that comes through for the genre itself, and the writers that came before. Mocking can be a kind of flattery. Shall we talk about Anna Brook-Mitchell’s Motherfaker? This novel has a great concept. I’ve heard of fake relationship novels, but fake pregnancy is a new one on me.

Well, if you want a how-to guide, I know now that in order to fake a pregnancy you need a variety of sizes of fake stomachs.

As soon as you say it, I think: Of course.

And you will probably need to bond with these different stomachs by giving them names when you wear them. That would help.

The main character is a teacher, who is becoming increasingly infuriated by the cult of the child in her workplace – the fact that her colleagues keep taking maternity leave or leaving her to do all the work while they attend baby yoga or sports days. Through a variety of circumstances, she ends up pretending to be pregnant. So, it’s a concept driven novel focussing on what happens when a scenario gets out of control. That’s quite intriguing, I guess, because in some ways being pregnant is rather out of one’s control.

Again, Brook-Mitchell is super good on physical comedy. And as you said, we often have plots involving people “passing” for different identity categories. But I’ve never encountered one about passing as pregnant.

But the book does have a core of sadness and anger to it. There is something both hilarious and deeply plangent about someone taping latex imaginary futures to themselves, about conjuring a baby.

It feels quite timely, with the rise of the child-free movement. By taking the idea to a comedic extreme, does it force us to some new thinking on the subject?

Yes. It connects with a great book by Sarah Knott, Mother Is A Verb. I think it does try to remind us – in a light way – that to mother is to nurture, and that this is open to everyone, not the domain of a particular few.

Thank you. Can we talk about the fifth book on the 2026 Wodehouse Prize shortlist? This is Offseason by Avigayl Sharp, a novel set in an all-girls boarding school. This was completely new to me.

So this is wild. Offseason is offbeat, off key. The narrator, heroine, is also a teacher. She’s been hired to cover teach for a term at a private school in a remote town on US coastal seaboard. It’s the off season there, so it’s quite empty, bleak and dark. But I guess the ‘off season’ also reminds us of the theatrical nature of what it means to be, or not to be, acting a role. And there’s a lot of comedy and tragedy in this novel about the roles and games people play. It’s also hugely focused on questions of negotiating trauma, and there’s a biting wit in relation to that.

She’s just dropped out of her PhD, our heroine-narrator, and there are there are some standout comic scenes about teaching. Like when she tries to correct a basic error made by a student, and her charge starts to ‘weep openly. Tears ran from the corner of her eyes down to her mouth, where her tongue flicked out automatically to lap them up’. Our narrator then furiously back-pedals, ‘I quickly tried to think of tender remarks that would make Anita stop crying so that I would not get fired and have to move back in with my parents’. The deadpan comic rhythm of that sentence, which moves from compassion to narcissism gives you a sense of this book.

And I also thought this was an interesting book, politically. It has two ghost texts underneath it: Bleak House – the class set text. And Sharp, like Dickens, is interested in who gets to be a main character and who doesn’t, in the people that cities ‘forget’. Meanwhile, it also has an epigraph from The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie. And there’s a lot, in this novel, as with Spark, about searching for a hero, for a story, for a meta-narrative, to find one’s way.

I’d say that the thing that makes this novel so particularly dark is that you spend all the time in our heroine’s mind. Actually, almost all of these books are in the first person in one way or another, but this is a mind that you’re quite glad to get out of.

She’s described as giving “manic” lectures.

Yes, you’re in the intensity of her thoughts, and those thoughts are, well, messy and full of snot and vomit and sex.

I think that might bring us to the final book on the shortlist, which is Mona Awad’s We Love You, Bunny. It’s described as ‘horror-satire’ which is an intriguing mash-up.

Yes. I’d say dark academia. Donna Tartt crossed with Alice in Wonderland, performed by the cast of Heathers.

I’m listening.

It’s about a group of obsessive MFA students who are holding hostage one of their former cohort. They are all telling their stories. The plot is centrally about storytelling, and in some ways you could see it as a sort of working-out of what Faulkner said about killing your darlings. (And these narrators are all, literally, darlings. They are all concerned with writing and floral prints and satin and nail polish, and they call each other ‘Bunny.’ ) Again, it’s very intense, completely absurd, magical realist.

They’re on a MFA course, and they are all comparing what the professor has fed back on what they have produced and performing their responses to it. One says:

How I cried and cried in the rose garden about his formatting comments. Actually totally inconsolable. How dare he suggest that I change the shape of my story? That I break up my paragraph further? It’s like he’s insisting I change the shape of me or something.

I did love this. Each of the narrators, as they are talking through what has happened, touches on the idea of the writing ego and the idea of inspiration. So I found this absurd and completely unexpected.

The MFA workshop format is ripe for a good comedy of manners.

Yes. And there are a lot of campus novels here on this list. Many of our list were, it seems, drawn to that sense of the closed world and its potential playing out big ethical questions of how we manage to be human and how we connect with other people. In Offseason we have the boarding school; in Motherfaker, she’s also a teacher.

Black Bag is set in a university. Then there’s this.

I was intrigued by that common thread. The campus with its potential for playing out ethical and imaginative questions. In We Love You, Bunny, it’s ego and creativity. In Black Bag, perhaps it’s big questions of how we connect with other people.

Right. In a closed community, you can allow the pressure to build until it becomes absurd. Otherwise, would you offer any other takeaways from the judging process? Did you find it easy or hard to come to a consensus?

There was a lot of consensus in what we were looking for. What I enjoyed about the group was that someone would say, oh, this is funny, and another person would be able to speak to the construction of it – something that explains why it is funny, which you had felt in your heart but hadn’t seen. That’s what I really enjoyed.

In some sense, I think the judging process was not so much one of resolving disagreement but of helping each other shed light on articulating why each book should be on the shortlist. All the books on there are brilliantly written and constructed, and independently we came to the same decisions – and together we were able to justify that.

I do feel these books are friends. They are not rivals, but compatriots. And so in some ways it will just be about deciding which best fits the bill for this prize. We’re a convivial bunch and I know we won’t leave the room until everyone is in total agreement.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

November 24, 2026

entries.title: Best New Science Books for Children: Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize 2026, recommended by Cristina Lazzeroni
entries.summary: The Royal Society Young People's Book Prize recognises the best new science books for kids, books that combine scientific accuracy with originality. Professor Cristina Lazzeroni, physicist and chair of the 2026 judging panel, introduces the exceptional titles on this year’s shortlist, and explains why they will inspire children to read about science. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
recommended by Cristina Lazzeroni

The Royal Society Young People's Book Prize recognises the best new science books for kids, books that combine scientific accuracy with originality. Professor Cristina Lazzeroni, physicist and chair of the 2026 judging panel, introduces the exceptional titles on this year’s shortlist, and explains why they will inspire children to read about science.

For those who haven’t come across the Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize before, can you introduce it and explain what kinds of books you are looking for?

The Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize recognises the best science writing for children under fourteen. The aim is to promote science literacy in young people, and to inspire them to read about science. The shortlist is selected by an adult panel, but the thing that makes this prize special is that the winner is voted by judging panels of young people, at schools, science centres, and community groups across the United Kingdom. Last year, votes were cast by over 11,000 young people, making up around 600 judging panels.

There are so many excellent science books today written for young people. What we look for in the books is that they combine accurate science with originality. For example, that they introduce an unusual topic, bring a novel perspective to a topic, or have an imaginative approach.

You are the Chair of the judging panel this year. Can you briefly introduce your own work and the background of the rest of the judging panel?

I’m a particle physicist. My research is based on experiments of very high precision, with the aim to enhance our understanding of physics at the smallest distances. I like the fact that it links to mathematics and to fundamental concepts, for example symmetries, which are everywhere.

The shortlisting panel consisted of four people in addition to me. They are: Andrew Blair, who is a primary school teacher and science subject leader; Dr Joshua Kestel, a Royal Society Newton International Fellow, who studies the relation between plants and pollinators; Hiba Noor Khan, who is an award-winning children’s book author and a former teacher of physics; and Ken Wilson-Max, who is also an award-winning children’s book author, and is an illustrator and publisher. We worked well together because we had different perspectives, different areas of expertise, and broad ranges of experience in engaging with children and with the public in general. For example, Joshua and I cover very different areas of science; Hiba and Ken could highlight key features of illustrations, with insights from having produced books themselves; and Andrew often commented on the qualities of a book that would appeal to children in classes that he’d taught.

Let’s go through the books that have been shortlisted for the 2026 Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize. Shall we start with the one for the youngest readers, The Great Pollination Investigation, by Deborah Hocking?

This is such a beautiful book, and the illustrations are magnificent. There are lots of interactive surprises, things that unfold. The 3D elements are excellent, and there is a bit of a collage style, which is a nice touch. The text font is large enough for a young audience, and the science is introduced in a way that makes it easy to follow. It keeps its interest from beginning to end.

It is very lovely. I saw that it’s fact-checked by the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, which is a good seal of approval. There is no upper age limit for this book, is there?

There is absolutely no upper age limit. I enjoyed The Great Pollination Investigation enormously. I’d say that there’s no age limit either side for any of the books shortlisted.

Next up of the shortlisted science books for kids is Elements of the Day by Samantha Lewis, illustrated by Hao Hao. Can you introduce it?

The concept of this book is great. It links everyday experiences to the periodic table of elements — something that most children encounter at some stage, but often in a quite abstract way. Elements of the Day makes the periodic table tangible and approachable. It’s fast paced and there’s a fair amount of humour and bizarreness peppered through the book, helping keep it interesting. It has a good mix of visuals and text, and is really accessible. It can encourage even the most-reluctant pupils to engage with the periodic table, helping them see the amazing role that it has outside of school.

It’s a great concept. I saw that a companion volume has just come out called Forces of the Day.

That’s good! Hopefully, it will be a candidate for next year’s Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize.

It really is. Again, this is a cool concept, introducing science with the help of magic. This can be a route into science for children who might initially be a bit put off by the subject. The collection of experiments is fantastic — I want to do them all! The committee could see children picking up this book because of the magic, then engaging with the science, reflecting on why the experiments work the way they do, and investigating further by themselves. They can try different experiments on different days, working through them at their own pace. They could try some of the experiments at school, or in a different environment, to explore further the science behind them. The book can work in many ways.

Let’s move on to Cosmo Park, which is illustrated by Tom Dearie and written by Madeleine Finlay, who has been shortlisted for this prize before, with Beetles for Breakfast.

Cosmo Park has a different feel to it. It is a science book about cosmology and astrophysics, written as a comic book. This was a unique approach among the books that we looked at. It has a fair amount of science in it, delivered skilfully, but the story is not just a way to convey information; it holds up on its own.

Yes, it’s an adventure story about a girl called Kara and her cat, who get a tour of the hot topics in astrophysics, right?

Yes, exactly. The cartoons are brilliant and fun to read, and the illustrations are wonderful. We thought that this book could also appeal to children who prefer a more visual form of storytelling.

Next on the list is Choose Your Own Evolution. This is such a great idea! It’s written by Jules Howard, a zoologist who is clearly passionate about wildlife conservation, with art by Gordy Wright, who has illustrated many books about the natural world.

I agree, such a great idea! The approach here is that you choose your own adventure, taking control of where you want to go; you build your own journey through the history of evolution. You can become extinct quite rapidly, but you can also survive for millennia; it’s highly interactive. The narrative is also good, engaging with the story of each of the animals. This will clearly appeal to the dinosaur enthusiast, but I think it will also appeal to many others. I expect it to raise lively discussion in the young people’s judging panels.

It’s very engagingly written, and has already won a couple of awards this year.

Elements of this book are fictionalised. It makes the story quite personal for each of the animals, and I related to this. I must admit, I became extinct a few times, then went back and started again. The last two pages show the tree of evolution, so you can follow how different creatures evolved, rather than building a path yourself. It’s simplified, but it still gives a good idea.

I really, really like Moving to Mars. There are so many different things to consider when exploring the idea of moving to Mars. At the end of the book the idea is more approachable than it was at the beginning, because you feel you’ve considered carefully and scientifically so many aspects.

So after reading this book, do you feel it’s only matter of time before we colonise Mars?

Exactly, it might not be soon, but eventually I think that humans will start moving to Mars! There’s a good amount of science in the book, it’s confidently written, and it’s well organised throughout. I also like the visuals, which have a retro style, a clever contrast to the very idea of moving to Mars. There’s a variety of visual elements, with good use of graphics and sketches. It’s a book that you can read in one go from start to finish, or you can dip in and out, and look at different aspects at different times. This makes the book very readable, and I enjoyed it a lot.

I really liked this book, too. You can learn a lot of science and engineering from it, but it’s also genuinely very exciting.

I agree! It’s excellent!

A whole team of scientists and science writers and illustrators worked on it, and they have another book coming out this month called Moving to the Moon.

Which is closer, in many ways!

I was really blown away by how fun all the shortlisted books are, filled to the brim with illustrations, and great for learning about science. I also thought that they’re remarkably well produced, with the publishers involving science communicators and specialist science writers for children.

Yes, indeed. Great care with presentation was taken across almost all of the books submitted. In the best, text and illustration work extremely well together, and this is something we paid attention to.

Are there any fields of science that you wish had been better covered by the books submitted for the Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize this year?

Yes, this year there were definitely some branches of science that were less represented than others. For example, my particle physics, but also computer science, quantum mechanics, and condensed matter. It would be good to find a way to encourage more accessible books in these areas.

Can you talk a bit about your own work in communicating science to children?

I’m passionate about sharing my enthusiasm for particle physics with a broad audience of all ages. I’ve taken part in interactive events across England, and I’ve produced resources for schools. I’m especially proud of a project called Particle Physics for Primary Schools. Young children can be refreshingly open to new ideas, and can ask the most brilliant questions. They make you think. Trying to explain things from the basics, while keeping them engaging, is a good way of discovering what you yourself are able to convey, or not. It’s an interesting challenge.

I’ve also been an expert consultant on the Britannica All New Children’s Encyclopedia. It was a great experience to be part of creating a book, and very different from staging in-person activities.

Do you have anything to add about your experience of being on the judging panel?

I realised as a child that books were a way to experience many lives in parallel and many ideas all at once. Reading was a way for me to multiply what I could do and what I could experience. I was reminded of this by many of the books submitted for the Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize, and especially by our shortlisted books.

Even though there were so many excellent submissions, arriving at the shortlist was less challenging that I’d anticipated, because of how well panel members worked together. It was hard to eliminate books at the beginning, because there was so much variety and quality that our favourites included almost the entire longlist. But when we went through each book in detail together, and all panellists presented their opinions, it was illuminating. We could see people’s various experiences coming into action, with each person presenting points overlooked by others. Consensus was reached through exchanges of ideas, so that we arrived at a clear idea of our favourites of favourites, and by the end of the meeting we had our shortlist of six.

Being Chair of the judging panel for the 2026 Royal Society Young People’s Book Prize, and having the chance to read all the books that were submitted, has been an absolute pleasure for me. I’ve always loved books. When I was a child, I was a super-avid reader and I disliked anyone telling me that I shouldn’t read a particular book because it was too advanced, and unsuitable for me. In this competition, I liked very much that there was such a variety of books, that they can be understood at different levels, and that the authors and illustrators haven’t underestimated their young audiences. The books here are for everybody.

I’ll be thrilled to discover the book that the children’s judging panels choose as their winner. I loved all of the books. I’m glad not to have to choose the best from the six books shortlisted, because I’d find this extremely difficult.

Cristina Lazzeroni

Cristina Lazzeroni is an experimental particle physicist who has had lead roles in kaon physics experiments at CERN. She also leads initiatives to make contemporary particle physics accessible to the wider public, and has been awarded the Lise Meitner Medal of the Institute of Physics for contributions to public engagement. She is Professor of Particle Physics, School of Physics and Astronomy, at the University of Birmingham, UK, and a Fellow of the Royal Society. She has published over 100 papers in international scientific journals.

entries.title: The Best Business Books of 2026: the Financial Times Business Book of the Year Award, recommended by Andrew Hill
entries.summary: The annual Financial Times Business Book of the Year Award, now in its third decade, celebrates books offering the most compelling and enjoyable insight into today's business issues—broadly defined. FT journalist Andrew Hill, organiser of the prize, talks us through the books that made this year's shortlist, from the perils of prophecy to the realities of the race for superintelligence. This inter
entries.content:
We’ve been covering the FT Business Book of the Year Award for a number of years, but for anybody who is new to it, could you explain what the prize is and what kind of business books you’re looking for?

The Financial Times has been running a business book award since 2005. The criteria remain roughly as they were then, which is that we’re looking for the most compelling and enjoyable insight into today’s business issues. Today’s business issues have certainly changed since 2005, but that is the prime criterion for picking a business book. Over the years, we’ve added a secondary criterion, which is that the winning book should stand the test of time, which is a very hard thing to predict, particularly in a world of fast-moving technology.

It’s worth saying that the breadth of the book award, right from the beginning, has been wider than what you might find on the business book shelves in a bookstore. We’ve tended to range from biography and history through to the traditional management books that you might find on that shelf, as well as embracing economics, technology, climate change, and so on.

With a team of Financial Times journalists that I help to coordinate, we pick 15 or 16 longlisted books, and then our expert judges pick a shortlist of six, which is where we are now. Then, in December, they will pick and award a winner. So that’s how it works.

In terms of business books in general, what trends have you seen over the past year?

The obvious trend of the last four or five years has been technology, specifically AI. Of the last six winners, five of them have been technology-related, so that’s clearly fed through into the award. It’s led to some really interesting conversations among the judges about what stands the test of time. If you’ve got a snapshot of AI today—which clearly is not going to be AI in five years’ time—to what degree does that snapshot still seem relevant later? That’s one of the running conversations we’ve been having.

There’s also been a subtheme which has run through everything of geopolitics, particularly in the last two or three years. As it happens, this has been a rare year when there were no books on the longlist that, for example, tackled China directly—or even indirectly, unless you count some of the AI books. But the growing global geopolitical and geoeconomic tension has been one of the themes that’s been prevalent in the last few years.

So those are probably the main trends.

The other thing worth mentioning is the tension that there always is between a really great narrative and a book that is heavy-duty economic or business analysis. That’s something that always plays out between the judges. Some of them prefer the journalistic narrative, and some of them prefer the ‘What have I got to really chew on here if I’m a chief executive?’

Let’s go through the books—I’ll take them in the order they are on the Financial Times website. So the first one is a work of economic history. This is 1873: The First Great Depression, and the Making of the Modern World. Will you tell me a bit about this one?

It’s worth mentioning first of all that the longlist this year had three former winners on it. One of them is the author of 1873, Liaquat Ahamed, whose book Lords of Finance won back in 2009. Both Lords of Finance, which was about the Depression era central bankers, and this book have echoes in current world affairs.

It’s a book about the first great global financial crisis of 1873. And, although Liaquat Ahamed does not make a huge deal out of this, clearly there are parallels between the 1873 crisis and the state of the geoeconomic world today: There was a big euphoric build-up. The financial system had recently modernised and globalised so that there was more debt being issued systematically. There were new technologies—in 1873’s case, railways, but also, subsea cables, which led to a big investment surge in infrastructure—which is paralleled by data centres and AI today. And it all came crashing down in 1873.

The book is full of little insights into the characters and the catastrophes. For example, I didn’t know that it was the Viennese stock market that collapsed, down by 45% in one day in May 1873. Better known is Jay Cooke’s investment bank in the U.S., which collapsed and started a domino effect.

There are lots of characters in there, both financial—the Rothschilds loom very large as the banking family that was organising a lot of the debt issuance—but there’s also Mark Twain, Karl Marx, and various exotic speculators around the world.

It has that sense of, ‘Here’s a cautionary tale from the past, one that you might not know, even if you know about the 1929 crash or Black Monday in 1987 or the global financial crisis of 2008.’ 1873 is not a date that we have previously thought of unless we’ve been financial historians.

And are there any tips in there that we can learn from—about what to do or what not to do?

I’m reluctant to sound fatalistic about it, but we are where we are. It’s hard to show how we would come out of where we are, other than through some kind of correction. There were issues with the speed with which railways and cables were built out, and clearly that has its parallels in the madcap rush to invest in AI infrastructure. So the attempts by some of the AI companies now to say, ‘Look, maybe we should slow down a little’—partly because they are themselves running up massive debts to build out the promised land—that does have a parallel with exaggerated investment in railway infrastructure, for example.

But you, as the reader, draw those lessons. The book doesn’t explicitly point to those lessons saying, ‘This is how one might do it today.’ I’m sure that Liaquat Ahamed will be asked all about that, or is being asked all about that. But like his previous book, it’s a rather beautiful, and beautifully written, history from which we are to draw our own cautionary tale.

Brilliant. Let’s go on to the next book, which is Off the Scales, billed in the subtitle as ‘the inside story of Ozempic and the race to cure obesity.’ This sounds interesting. What can you tell me about this book?

This is by Aimee Donnellan. It is about Ozempic—the product which was Novo Nordisk’s patented weight loss drug—but it’s not just about that; it’s also about the entire cultural and pharmaceutical revolution that that set off. Ozempic was the initial discovery that got people looking into it, but it’s led to Wegovy, Mounjaro and others.

It’s about the chemistry and the discovery of GLP-1 drugs, which is the generic name for them, and the scientists behind that. It also tells us about the ways in which Novo Nordisk’s own fortunes were affected by the discovery. Some of the reviews have pointed out that by focusing on Novo Nordisk, the book tends to leave out the more successful drugs that compete in that market, like Mounjaro, which is an Eli Lilly drug.

The discovery has clearly made a huge cultural difference. It’s very hard to have a conversation these days without somebody pointing to the benefits, either for themselves or for unnamed others, of being able to use the weight loss drugs, and indeed some of the downsides, which have spilled over into everything from restaurant bookings to portion sizes. There is a sort of cultural history built into the book.

It is a classic business cultural commentary book, and it’s got a broad brief to talk about everything related to obesity: What caused the crisis? Why are we so hung up about it? What are the ways in which advertising has contributed? There is the shame of obesity, but also the pride in beating obesity, and how that feeds into this story.

It’s a very broad take on what, at root, is an extraordinary pharmaceutical discovery.

The book starts very nicely, with a story of someone at work who’s suddenly getting promoted and lots of attention, and the only thing that’s changed is that she’s lost lots of weight after taking it, right?

Exactly. Immediately, a value judgement is being applied to somebody’s personal choices, which not everyone might be able to make. That feeds through to the whole story. What the dinner party discussion might focus on—though dinner parties might possibly also be a victim of appetite inhibition drugs—is: are you obese through your own choices, or is it something that you can avoid? The existence of a magic pill that you can take puts all those things into sharp relief.

Editor’s note: Off the Scales is called The Hunger Game: The Inside Story of GLP-1s and the Race to Cure Obesity in its paperback edition, out on November 19, 2026

Up next we have one of the AI books. What can you tell me about The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind and the Quest for Superintelligence?

This is the other book on the shortlist by a previous winner, Sebastian Mallaby. He seems to have an ability to hit the target for the FT Business Book Award — he’s had a number of shortlisted books and won back in 2016 for The Man Who Knew, his big biography of Alan Greenspan, the former Federal Reserve chair.

This is again a book centred on a single personality with a huge influence: Demis Hassabis, co-founder of DeepMind, which now belongs to Google, and winner of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the protein folding work that he did using AI. Hassabis is one of the seven or eight great visionaries about artificial intelligence.

The book traces the life of Hassabis and the evolution of DeepMind and there are some fascinating biographical details in there. Hassabis was an extraordinary chess prodigy, but decided, eventually, ‘What are we doing using our brains to play chess all the time when we could be solving the problems of humanity?’

Hassabis comes across very much as a good visionary. He thinks AI will be good for the world, but I must admit I came away from the book a little depressed. Towards the end, Hassabis essentially says, ‘We are in a race. It’s a race to see who wins this, and DeepMind is part of the race.’ We’ve heard a lot about the dangers of AI in recent months, and DeepMind is contributing to that arms race that some warn might end in catastrophe.

Mallaby has taken a similar approach to his previous books, which is that he’s done a lot of interviews with Hassabis and woven his book around what Hassabis himself says about artificial intelligence. Presciently, it’s called ‘superintelligence’ in the subtitle, having second-guessed Trump’s attempt to make us all refer to it as that.

Mallaby presumably finished interviewing Hassabis last year. He has since moved to a different job at DeepMind, slightly out of the line of fire. And of course we have had the extraordinary story about Jensen Huang – the subject of last year’s winner The Thinking Machine – resigning from Nvidia after an affair with a Chinese woman suspected of spying for China’s state intelligence agency. So The Infinity Machine poses an interesting question for the judges. They’ll have to consider not only whether they will pick another AI book, but also whether what Hassabis said will stand the test of time.

Hassabis wants to be optimistic about the options. I came away deeply pessimistic about the potential outcomes, but it is a brilliantly written portrait of a brilliant man at a time of extraordinary technological change.

I was reading John Thornhill’s review of the book, and he mentioned that it is not only a biography of Hassabis, but also shows the evolution of AI research over the last 25 years. So, if you want to know about that, it might be quite a good book to read as well.

Yes, that’s right. I think Hassabis is a great lens through which to watch this. Apart from having won the Nobel Prize for an obvious beneficial use of AI, Hassabis was also at the top of DeepMind when it beat the masters of the ancient Asian game Go. He is somebody who has, for a long time, had to consider the trade-offs that you have to make between the commercialisation and the vision.

So, seen through him and through DeepMind, quite a lot of the rest of the world of AI falls into place. It’s a big book, so as well as DeepMind itself, there’s also plenty of room for Mallaby to explain what the competitors are doing.

Let’s go on to the next book: Project Maven: A Marine Colonel, His Team, and the Dawn of AI Warfare, which opens with that moment when a computer beats the world’s top player of Go. Is this another scary book?

Yes, this is a scary book. We had a book on our shortlist in 2024 called Unit X, which was about how the Pentagon and Silicon Valley are transforming the future of war. Two years later we’re in a war, and Katrina Manson—who is a former colleague at the Financial Times—has dug deep into this story about how the Pentagon has taken on AI tools in order to create these frightening, potentially autonomous weapons.

She’s built the book around a colonel, Drew Cukor, who has been at the tip of the spear in Project Maven, which is the name of the operation to get AI into combat.

‘Is this a business book?’ you might ask. But it brings in the fact that all the big companies—even the ones that are trying to play nice, like Anthropic—have Pentagon contracts. Palantir, which is in the news here in the UK because of its involvement with the NHS, is clearly one of the companies that has benefited from being at the spearhead of this technology, and algorithms from other companies like Microsoft are also involved.

The book covers, to some degree, the pushback from within the technology industry—the workers at Google who objected to being involved in the project.

It’s very up to the minute and topical because there’s a lot of discussion going on about the future of warfare. I mentioned that there weren’t any China books on this year’s shortlist, but this is obviously a book that implicitly and explicitly talks about how AI is being thrown into the battle for military dominance, where China’s own military ambitions play very strongly. And clearly, to some extent, this is also a Trump book because the Trump administration is gung-ho behind developing military technology and becoming—or cementing itself as—the most powerful AI-powered military in the world.

Is there an example of what might happen if AI is heavily involved in combat?

I tend to think about the autonomous weapons. That was the cause of Anthropic wanting to pull back from dealing with the Pentagon. Its contract seemed to be drawn up to allow the Pentagon simply to use its AI models to do what it wanted with autonomy, without any intervention, and that was worrying. The book shows just how far militaries have come in developing swarms of autonomous weaponised drones that could be deployed in conflicts not so far in the future.

Let’s go on to Blood Will Flow: The Murderous Business of Oil and Gas. I initially thought this was going to be about oil and gas in general, but it’s focused on a very specific event in Mozambique. Do you want to tell me what it’s about and why it made the shortlist?

This is a real page-turner, the book that’s probably closest to a thriller. It’s also a really splendid piece of reporting.

Alex Perry, the author, has gone to track down everybody who was affected or involved—insofar as they still are around to talk to him—in a rampage by Islamist militants through a town in northern Mozambique in 2021. That prompted the big French energy company TotalEnergies to suspend its offshore natural gas project there, and to have to fight claims that it didn’t do enough to protect its subcontractors. I should say Total denies those claims.

From this—and also going back into history—he builds a picture of the human damage that the fossil fuel industry has done over its 20th- and 21st-century history. He uses the Mozambique example as a way to demonstrate the almost unnoticed damage that has been done. A lot of the people who were killed and that he’s spoken to were the workers and subcontractors who were the little people in this big picture.

There is a very big person in the book as well, who is still the CEO of TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné. He is painted as this extraordinary alpha male fossil fuel executive with Napoleonic powers at the top of Total. As I say, the company denies what Perry alleges, but the book is a powerful counterweight to the public marketing of oil and gas companies.

I felt sad at the beginning, when he’s interviewing local officials, and one of them says, ‘We thought when they found gas, it would be a good thing for our community.’ Instead, it brought death and destruction.

The allegation is that the oil and gas compound itself—which was within reach of being able to assist—didn’t send any of the big protection forces that it had to help out. The idea that runs through the book is that there is this sealed-off world of oil and gas that discovers, extracts, and makes large amounts of money, and that beyond those fences, beyond the boundaries of those companies, people suffer.

The publicity for the book says it delivers a morality tale, and the book does, in a large sense, draw this depressing moral.

Let’s turn to the final book on this year’s shortlist. This is Prophecy: Prediction, Power, and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI by Carissa Véliz, who is based at the Institute for Ethics in AI here in Oxford.

Prophecy has a completely different flavour from every other book on the list. She goes back to the Greeks and the oracles of Delphi, that’s one of her interesting starting points and talks about prophecy and old-fashioned prophets. She gives some very acute insights into why we shouldn’t be as trusting as we are of so-called accurate forecasts.

Again, we always pose the question: ‘Is it a business book?’ Very clearly it is, because not only does it talk about prediction in business in general, it goes quite deep into insurance industry forecasting and is right up to date in terms of what’s built into the algorithms that are driven by AI.

It’s a very sceptical look at what happens when we believe or become too focused on predictions. Her line is essentially that forecasting has always been about people exerting power, and that one should be very careful before you swallow predictions. These days, of course, we don’t necessarily even know when we are subject to the predictions built into algorithms. We should be very careful and ask the question: ‘What are we actually being pointed to here, and why?’

It’s quite a personal book. There’s quite a lot of her own experience. It’s written in an extremely lively and unpredictable way, which I think is a virtue here. It has a lot of interesting insights about the pitfalls of prediction and the ways in which prediction has led us down the wrong track.

She’s a philosopher. In that sense, it’s a bit of a step away from the journalists who often dominate our shortlist. It’s nice to have somebody who is an intellectual thinker in a different discipline from economics or business on this occasion.

Is there an example you could give from the book?

There’s this bit where she introduces her own agent, Andrew Wiley. He talks about his distrust of the data and of authors who predict their own books will be bestsellers. He prefers to focus on the quality and the enduring value of the book. That introduces a longer discussion of how, by reading ebooks, we are simply feeding data to Amazon and giving power to profit-driven companies that want to drive us away from physical books.

Thanks so much, Andrew, for talking us through these books.

It’s an exciting list. It’s different from previous years. It’s going to be intriguing to see which book wins.

The winner of the 2026 Financial Times and Standard Chartered Business Book of the Year Award will be announced on Wednesday, December 2, 2026.
